name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,900

clue.text: Greens in US enjoying great popularity now lead

blocks.note: American money is green, and a greenback is a buck
a hot ticket is the one everybody wants at the moment

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are slang for something other than shooting: dollars and fashionability. 'Lead' is the metal, not the verb, which is why it can sit at the end looking like a job description.
explanation.definitionFit: lead → BUCKSHOT: buckshot is the coarse lead pellets a shotgun cartridge is loaded with, so the metal names the shot made of it.

clue.text: No chicken sandwiches in Washington? What an idea!

indicators.note: To sandwich a filling is to shut it between two slices, so the outer word splits and takes the rest inside.

blocks.note: a chicken is a coward, so no chicken is brave
IN taken as itself, then WA, the postal abbreviation for Washington state

explanation.walkthrough: Two American conventions in five words: the state abbreviation WA, and 'chicken' for a coward. The exclamation mark belongs to the definition, not to the surface's outrage.
explanation.definitionFit: What an idea! → BRAINWAVE: a brainwave is the sudden bright idea that greets exactly that exclamation, not the electrical trace neurologists measure.

clue.text: Dismiss employee always putting their hand in the till

definitions.text: employee always putting their hand in the till

blocks.note: the military sense: to strip an officer of rank and turn them out

blocks.clueFragment: employee always putting their hand in the till
blocks.note: the shop sense, where a hand in the till is the job rather than the crime

explanation.walkthrough: The joke lives in 'always': a till-dipping employee sounds like a thief, and the second definition is describing somebody entirely honest doing their work.
explanation.definitionFit: To cashier an officer is to dismiss them from the service in disgrace; a cashier in a shop is the worker whose hands belong in the till.

clue.text: Old luvvie girl judges on all but the last of his plays

indicators.note: To play a part is to appear as somebody you are not, and these letters appear as a name that is not their own order.
It keeps everything except the closing letter, so the word joins the mix one short.

blocks.note: twelve of the fourteen letters, taken as they stand

blocks.clueFragment: all but the last of his
blocks.note: HIS gives up its S, adding the last two letters to the pile

explanation.walkthrough: A fourteen-letter anagram hides best when its fodder reads as ordinary sense — a girl judging a playwright's work — and when the indicator is the theatrical word 'plays'.
explanation.definitionFit: Old luvvie → SIR JOHN GIELGUD: 'luvvie' is British slang for a grandly theatrical actor, and he was the most celebrated of the knighted stage generation.

clue.text: Did boss make too deep cuts?

blocks.note: English marks excess with the prefix over-, so going too far is going over
a saw is what makes cuts, and the tool's name serves as the verb

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a manager asked about redundancies; the wordplay is a carpenter's blunder. The answer only turns into a past tense once the two pieces are read as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Did boss → OVERSAW: to oversee work is to be in charge of it, and the clue's 'Did' asks for that verb in the past.

clue.text: Piece made by sculptor completely out of dough

blocks.note: the head-and-shoulders portrait in stone or bronze
broke — dough being money, and the slang for having none of it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dough' does two jobs at once: it belongs with the sculptor's modelling material on the surface, and it means cash in the definition that counts.
explanation.definitionFit: A bust is the sculpted head and shoulders; the same word is slang for broke, so somebody entirely out of money is bust.

clue.text: Cut chance of losing in wager

indicators.note: The small word does the placing: what comes before it goes inside what comes after, rather than beside it.

blocks.note: a wager is a bet, and it is the word that opens up
the chance of losing something is the risk you run

explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is about gambling and none of it is about meat. The one butcher's word in the clue is sitting at the very front.
explanation.definitionFit: Cut → BRISKET: brisket is the butcher's cut from the animal's breast, so the general word defines it as one cut among many.

clue.text: Steps taken by proletariat succeeded in revolution

definitions.note: 'Steps' is plural and the answer singular: a stair is the whole flight, so one stair is made of many steps.

indicators.note: What a phrase takes is carried inside it, so the letters are lifted out of the words exactly as they stand.
A revolution turns a thing right round, so the run of letters has to be read the other way about.

blocks.note: the letters run across the join — proleta|RIAT S|ucceeded — and they arrive turned round

explanation.walkthrough: A revolution by the proletariat is such a natural phrase that nothing in it looks like an instruction, which is exactly the cover a buried answer needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Steps → STAIR: a stair is a flight of steps taken as one thing — 'up the stair' — rather than a single tread.

clue.text: Representative upset being limited by sex, so neutral?

indicators.note: In a down entry, upsetting the pile sends what was written at the foot of it up to the top.
To be limited by a thing is to have it as your edge, so the two words finish flush against each other rather than one inside the other.

blocks.note: a being is a person — 'human being' with the human left off
congress is the formal word for sexual intercourse, as in carnal congress
no letters: the setter's nod to why this ending exists, standing in for the two gendered titles

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is about sex twice over — the act, and the grammatical kind the answer is designed to avoid. Only one of those meanings puts letters in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Representative → CONGRESSPERSON: a member of the US House is formally styled a Representative, so the definition names the office by its holder's title.

clue.text: Spoils of war?

definitions.note: 'of war' does not define a word so much as point at the Roman god of it; the setter leaves 'god' unsaid so the phrase 'spoils of war' can stay whole.

blocks.note: the plain verb: to mar a thing is to spoil it, and this is the third person
the Roman god, whose name the red planet also carries

explanation.walkthrough: Four letters and a famous phrase: the setter has written nothing but 'spoils of war' and split it in the one place that turns plunder into a deity.
explanation.definitionFit: To mar is to spoil, so the verb's third person is one reading; the other is the Roman god war itself was named after.

clue.text: Using persuasive language that might make you a lot richer

indicators.note: 'Make' here means turn into: the letters are being turned into something they are not yet, so they cannot stay as they are.

blocks.note: the ten letters of A LOT RICHER, dealt again

explanation.walkthrough: Persuasive language really might make you richer, so the surface holds together perfectly and gives you no reason to count the letters of the last three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Using persuasive language → RHETORICAL: rhetoric is the ancient art of persuasion, so rhetorical describes speech shaped to win an audience round.

clue.text: Half grudgingly admired golf club's location

definitions.note: The answer is a plural-only noun — environs are the surrounding district — while 'location' is singular; the setter names the district by the single place it rings.

indicators.note: Only the front portion of the word is wanted, three letters out of the six that grudging admiration spells.

blocks.note: to admire grudgingly is to have ENVIED, and half of that six-letter word is its first three
an iron is the metal-headed golf club
the apostrophe-s of 'club's' is taken as a plain letter

explanation.walkthrough: A golf club's location reads as a course address, and the clue means nothing of the kind. Watch for a possessive being cashed in as a letter — setters do it constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: location → ENVIRONS: the environs of a town are the ground immediately round it, so the word names a place by the district it occupies.

clue.text: Racer finally demonstrating good skill

indicators.note: It asks for the very end of the word beside it, one letter and no more.

blocks.note: its final letter, which is what 'finally' asks for
OK is the everyday word for good enough
art in the sense of a mastered craft, as in the art of conversation

explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration (2-4) tells you the answer is hyphenated, and the wordplay pays that hyphen no attention at all. Note too that 'finally' sits before its word rather than after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Racer → GO-KART: a go-kart is a small open-framed racing car, so the definition names it by the only thing it is built for.

clue.text: Producing no crops, to do with farm storage limits

indicators.note: To set the limits of a thing is to stand at both ends of it, so the outer word opens and takes the other inside.

blocks.note: the barn is where a farm keeps its harvest, and it is the word that splits
re means concerning, the word at the head of a memo

explanation.walkthrough: A barn stands for farm storage so readily that it never looks like a container, and 'limits' passes as part of the same phrase about capacity.
explanation.definitionFit: Producing no crops → BARREN: barren land is soil too poor to yield a harvest, the farming sense of the word rather than the human one.

clue.text: Small layer you hear, little songbird

indicators.note: What you hear is a sound and not a spelling, so the words are to be taken by ear and written down differently.

blocks.note: small is wee and a layer of a cake is a tier; run the two together and the sound is the bird's name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Layer' pulls hard towards a hen, which is the wrong kind of layer entirely — the setter wants the layer of a cake. The bird has nothing to do with wheat or with ears.
explanation.definitionFit: little songbird → WHEATEAR: the wheatear is a small chat of open moorland, and 'songbird' places it by family rather than naming it.

clue.text: Military leader's old mate aboard American Eagle?

indicators.note: Anything taken aboard travels inside the vessel, so these letters ride within the word around them.

blocks.note: Apollo 11's Eagle was a lunar module — a lander, and an American one; the question mark admits it is an example
an ex is the partner you used to have

explanation.walkthrough: 'American Eagle' reads as a bird, an airline or a coin, and the setter means a spacecraft. Once the Eagle is a lander, the indefinite article in front of it is doing real work.
explanation.definitionFit: Military leader → ALEXANDER: it names a commander by example — Alexander the Great, and the Field Marshal Alexander of the Second World War.

clue.text: Let out water through conical structure

blocks.note: per is Latin for through, the sense kept in 'per capita'
a spire is the tapering cone on top of a church tower

explanation.walkthrough: Water running through a conical structure paints a fountain, and the answer is about skin. PER for 'through' is worth banking — it turns up in dozens of charades.
explanation.definitionFit: Let out water → PERSPIRE: perspiring is the body letting water out through the skin, which is simply sweating said politely.

clue.text: Deer charges around in charming animation

indicators.note: Sent around, a thing comes back the way it went, so the whole assembly is read from its far end.

blocks.note: the elk is the crossword's standard deer
a rap is a criminal charge — 'take the rap' — so charges are raps

explanation.walkthrough: Two little words carry the whole clue: 'charges' means accusations rather than a stampede, and the deer is not running anywhere. Turned round, the pair spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: charming animation → SPARKLE: sparkle is the liveliness of a person's manner, the same metaphor as calling a talker sparkling.

clue.text: Suffer humiliation, turning red at it

indicators.note: Milk that is turning is no longer what it was, and letters in the act of turning have not settled into their order yet.

blocks.note: the seven letters of RED AT IT, dealt again

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning red' is a blush, which is what humiliation looks like, so the indicator and its fodder read as a single idea. The answer is two words where the fodder is three.
explanation.definitionFit: Suffer humiliation → EAT DIRT: to eat dirt is the idiom for swallowing an insult without answering back, a whole phrase rather than a synonym.

clue.text: "Retreat," soldiers heading to the front communicated silently

indicators.note: In an across entry the front is the left-hand end, so letters that head there arrive in the opposite order.

blocks.note: a den is a private retreat, a bolt-hole rather than a withdrawal
GIs are American soldiers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Retreat' in quotation marks looks exactly like the order to turn about, and it is a hiding place instead. The turning is done by the march to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: communicated silently → SIGNED: to sign is to talk with the hands, in sign language or by gesture, which makes no sound at all.

clue.text: Fair beauty burdened by sentiment

indicators.note: A burden sits on top of whatever carries it, so in a down entry the load is written above the thing bearing it.

blocks.note: goo is sloppy sentimentality, the stuff a gooey film is made of
a dish is long-standing slang for a good-looking person

explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are slang, which is what lets the surface read as a straight sentence about somebody weighed down by feeling. A down entry's geometry sets the order.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair → GOODISH: the -ish weakens good to 'reasonably good', and 'fair' is the same grudging half-praise in a school report.

clue.text: Toff completely foul at Lord's

blocks.note: a nob is a swell, somebody of high social rank
all in the sense of wholly, as in 'all wrong'

explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is cricket's headquarters, so the foul in question is a bowling offence. 'Toff' and 'nob' are both Victorian words for the same well-dressed man.
explanation.definitionFit: foul at Lord's → NO-BALL: a no-ball is the bowler's illegal delivery, and naming the ground is the setter's way of saying the foul is a cricketing one.

clue.text: Saving pence, Capone doctored the drink

indicators.note: Saving here means 'except for', so the coin named next is held back rather than used.
A doctored document has been tampered with, and tampered-with letters no longer sit where they were put.

blocks.note: p is the abbreviation for pence, and it is the letter set aside
CAPONE without that p leaves five letters to be rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: Al Capone was a bootlegger, so a doctored drink is exactly the story the surface wants to tell, and none of it has anything to do with the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: the drink → OCEAN: 'the drink' is sailors' and airmen's slang for the sea, as in a plane ditching in the drink.

clue.text: Always taking the soft option?

blocks.note: the surface reading: somebody who never once risks the harder choice
at a bar the soft option is the drink with no alcohol in it, and taking it every time is a way of life

explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to find here — the whole clue is one description, and the step is realising that 'soft' is a bar word rather than a word about courage.
explanation.definitionFit: Always taking the soft option? → TEETOTAL: soft drinks are the ones without alcohol, so somebody who takes only those has sworn off drink altogether.

clue.text: Throwing loops of rope on board, pack square boxes first for once

definitions.text: Throwing loops of rope on board

indicators.note: To box a thing is to shut it in, so the word doing the boxing opens up and takes the other inside.
Only the opening letter of the word beside it is wanted, not the word itself.

blocks.note: a pack of cards is a deck of cards
to be quits with somebody is to be square with them, all debts settled
its opening letter alone

explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface is a packing job aboard ship, which is also where the game is played, so definition and wordplay are describing the same deck.
explanation.definitionFit: Throwing loops of rope on board → DECK QUOITS: quoits are rings pitched at a peg, and the shipboard version uses rope rings thrown along the deck.

clue.text: Motor races affected by gales not starting

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer names one meeting: 'the Indy' is used for the racing as a whole, not for a single afternoon's event.

indicators.note: A word that is not starting has lost its opening letter and begins one along.

blocks.note: weather affected by gales is WINDY, which here never gets to start

explanation.walkthrough: A race that never starts is the joke. The letter goes missing from the weather rather than from the race, which is what makes the surface hold together.
explanation.definitionFit: Motor races → INDY: the Indianapolis 500 is universally shortened to the Indy, and the name now covers the whole American open-wheel racing series.

clue.text: German teacher keeps money in pot, initially

indicators.note: What a phrase keeps, it holds on to inside itself, so the letters are already there in the words as written.

blocks.note: the run bridges the join between the two words, ending just past the start of the second

explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' looks like an instruction to take a first letter and is part of the definition instead — the stake goes in before any cards are dealt.
explanation.definitionFit: money in pot, initially → ANTE: the ante is the stake every player must put into the pot before a hand begins, so it is the pot's opening money.

clue.text: Report of a Russian ghost ship stopped in the Channel?

indicators.note: A report of something is the account you are given by ear, so what follows is to be heard rather than read.

blocks.note: Russia's sanctioned 'ghost fleet' is made of tankers, so a Russian ghost ship is a tanker — and 'a tanker' is what you hear

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a news bulletin about the shadow fleet. The trick is where the break falls in the sound: move it one letter along and the same syllables turn nautical.
explanation.definitionFit: stopped in the Channel? → AT ANCHOR: a vessel at anchor is held fast to the seabed and going nowhere, which for a ship is what being stopped means.
